title: RegExp
lede: PCRE2 under the hood, but aligned to the ECMAScript dialect by default so the everyday edge cases (`$` at the true end, an unset backreference matching empty, `\uXXXX` escapes) behave as real JS does. The recurring divergences are structural: strings are byte-indexed, so match offsets are byte positions unless you opt into `-regex=es-utf16`; result arrays narrow a truly-`null` optional capture to `""` and drop the `index`/`input`/`groups` extras; and `matchAll` is eager, not a lazy iterator. The whole-program `-regex=<mode>` flag trades fidelity for speed across five modes, and the `u`/`y`/`d` flags are out of scope for V1.

entries.name: Construction: new RegExp(pattern, flags?)
entries.signature: new RegExp(pattern: string, flags?: string): RegExp
entries.description: Compiles the pattern once via PCRE2 and throws a real, catchable SyntaxError on an invalid pattern. The flags string is validated as in real JS — a duplicate flag ("gg") or an unrecognized flag character ("z") throws a SyntaxError. A \uXXXX/\xXX escape compiles as an ECMAScript escape in the default and es-ascii modes.

entries.name: Literal syntax: /pattern/flags
entries.description: Regex literals desugar to the same construction at parse time. An unescaped '/' inside a [...] character class does not end the literal.
differences: `x in /foo/` mis-lexes the `/` as division (the lexer's regex-vs-division disambiguation gap, since `in` isn't its own token in this lexer) — a small, deliberately-accepted gap

entries.name: .source / .flags
entries.description: Plain field reads of the original constructor arguments, verbatim.
entries.snippet:
const r = new RegExp("^\\d+$", "gm")
console.log(r.flags) // gm

entries.name: .global / .ignoreCase / .multiline / .dotAll
entries.description: The four boolean flag accessors, decomposed from the flags string once at construction — no method needs to re-parse it.

returns.desc: Whether the corresponding flag is set.

entries.name: .lastIndex
entries.description: The iteration cursor: mutated by .exec()/.test()/global str.match()/str.matchAll()/str.replace()/str.replaceAll() (advances on a successful g-flagged match, resets to 0 after a failed one), and deliberately untouched by str.split()/str.search(), matching real JS.

entries.name: .test(str)
entries.description: A real PCRE2 match returning a boolean. A g-flagged RegExp reads/advances .lastIndex exactly as .exec() does, so a while (re.test(s)) loop steps through every match; a non-global RegExp always matches from offset 0 and never touches .lastIndex.

entries.name: .exec(str)
entries.description: Returns string[] | null — index 0 is the full match, 1..N are the numbered capture groups; real, working m !== null / if (m) checks against the result. A global RegExp reads/writes .lastIndex exactly like real JS, so the while ((m = re.exec(s)) !== null) idiom works. All matching methods route through the one compiled PCRE2 handle, so the -regex dialect mode applies uniformly here and to match/matchAll/replace/replaceAll/split/search.

returns.desc: Match array, or null on no match.

differences: An unmatched optional capture group becomes `""` rather than a true per-element `null` (no per-element-nullable-string array exists)
Real JS's `index`/`input`/`groups` extra properties on the result aren't built

entries.name: str.match(regexp)
entries.description: Without g: identical to regexp.exec(str). With g: full-match-only strings, and null (not []) on zero matches — matching real JS exactly.
differences: Shares `.exec()`'s result-array narrowing (an unmatched optional capture group becomes `""`, not per-element `null`; no `index`/`input`/`groups`)

entries.name: str.matchAll(regexp)
entries.description: One .exec()-shaped match array per match; throws TypeError without the g flag.
differences: Returns an eager `string[][]`, not a real lazy iterator (no lazy-iteration infrastructure exists anywhere in this compiler)

entries.name: str.replace(regexp, replacement)
entries.signature: str.replace(regexp: RegExp, replacement: string | ((m, offset, string) => string)): string
entries.description: Replaces the first match without g, every match with g; the callback runs exactly once per match.
entries.snippet:
console.log("range: 12-34 end".replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)/, "[$2:$1]")) // range: [34:12] end
console.log("a1 b22 c333".replace(/\d+/g, (m: string, offset: number) => m + "@" + offset))
differences: Replacement template supports `$1`-`$9`/`$&`/`$$` only (`` $` ``/`$'` — pre-/post-match text — are out of scope)

The callback form is invoked with a fixed `(match, offset, string)` — real JS's variadic `...capturedGroups` in the middle isn't supported (a callback's arity is fixed at compile time but a pattern's capture count is only known at runtime; a callback declaring more than 3 parameters is a compile-time error)

entries.name: str.replaceAll(regexp, replacement)
entries.signature: str.replaceAll(regexp: RegExp, replacement: string | ((m, offset, string) => string)): string
entries.description: Same replacement rules as .replace(); requires the g flag, throwing TypeError otherwise.
entries.snippet: console.log("cat dog cat".replaceAll(/cat/g, "DOG")) // DOG dog DOG
differences: Same replacement narrowing as `.replace()` (`$1`-`$9`/`$&`/`$$` only; fixed `(match, offset, string)` callback)

entries.name: str.split(regexp)
entries.description: Finds every match regardless of the g flag (its own local search loop, like real JS). A regex that never matches returns a single-element array holding the whole subject.
differences: Only splits on a non-zero-length match — real JS's more intricate zero-length-match handling isn't replicated
Captured groups in the split pattern are never spliced into the result (out of scope from the start)

entries.name: str.search(regexp)
entries.description: Always searches from offset 0, restores .lastIndex afterward — invisible to later .exec()/.test() iteration, matching real JS exactly. A plain-string argument is coerced to a RegExp as in real JS (metacharacters interpreted). Returns -1 on no match.

entries.name: u / y / d flags
entries.description: The u (unicode), y (sticky), and d (indices) flags are deferred for the whole feature's V1. \u{…} code-point escapes, surrogate handling, Unicode \p{…}/class semantics, and strict-syntax validation are a later option.
